<meta>continues from previous page: the neighborhood, and the mountains echoed with that howling. He was killed by casting huge rocks from the edges of the pit onto the stakes fixed into him. Even with his right paw fixed, he broke a thousand splinters and a thousand fragments of the spears aimed and hurled at him from above. Half-dead and drained of blood, he filled the onlookers with dread, wondering what he might have done if he were free and unharmed.</meta>

John Ledesma of Seville, a friend and companion in the labors of Vasco <note>Vasco Núñez de Balboa</note>, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported to me that it was in no way inferior to beef. When asked why they call it a tiger, those who have now seen the tiger respond that they judge it to be a tiger by its spots, its ferocity, its agility, and other signs given by authors. This is despite the fact that many of them claim to have seen both leopards and panthers, which are also spotted.

After the male tiger was killed, they followed its tracks toward the mountains and reached the bridal cave that was its home. <margin>On the nature of the tiger.</margin> In the mother's absence, they took away two cubs that were not yet old enough for their mother’s teats. Changing their plan so that they might later send them to Spain once they had grown larger, they carefully fitted iron chains around their necks and brought the little ones back to the mother's cave. Returning to the cave a few days later, they found the cave empty and the chains unmoved from their place. It is thought the mother, in her rage, tore them into pieces and carried them off so that no one else might enjoy them. For they assert that they could by no means have escaped the chains alive. The skin of the killed tiger was stuffed with dried herbs and straw and sent to Hispaniola for the admiration of the leading men from whom these lands expect laws and reinforcements. Both those who suffered hardships from the tiger and those who handled its skin have discussed these things with me; we accept what is given.

We must return to Pacra, from whom we had digressed. Having entered the deserted <term>boios</term> <gloss>houses</gloss> of Pacra, Vasco strove to draw Pacra out. Through messengers, he signaled to Pacra the same things we mentioned were signaled to the others. <margin>Pacra returns.</margin> For a long time Pacra refused. Threats were added to his refusal. At last he came, accompanied by three <term>reguli</term> <gloss>local chieftains</gloss>. Vasco writes that Pacra was so deformed, filthy, and foul that he confesses he never saw anything more shameful. <margin>What kind of man Pacra is; he is considered a Hercules.</margin> He says that nature gave him only a human form, but otherwise he was a wild, monstrous, brute animal. He says his character was equal to his habits and features. He had abused the daughters of four neighboring chieftains, whom he had taken by force, with detestable lust. Many other things of this sort concerning the obscene morals of Pacra and his crimes were boasted of by the neighboring chieftains before Vasco as if before a praetorian judge or, by Hercules, an avenger, so that punishment might be taken upon Pacra. <margin>What is done against the wicked.</margin> He cast that massive beast, along with the three chieftains who obeyed Pacra's word and suffered from the same vices, into the jaws of the war dogs, and ordered their mangled corpses to be burned.

Wonderful things are related concerning the dogs with which they enter battles. <margin>Wonders concerning the dogs.</margin> Against the armed natives, there was no need for swords or arrows or other weapons to rout the opposing enemies; for once the signal was given and the dogs were released, the column, terrified by the appearance and unusual barking of the Molossian dogs, would hesitate and, in confusion, abandon their battle lines and orders. It happens differently, however, when they engage with the Caramairenses and Caribs; for they are fiercer and more apt at waging wars. Charging, they aim their poisoned arrows at the dogs faster than a lightning strike, and kill many. The inhabitants of these mountains, however, do not wage war with arrows; <margin>With what weapons they wage war.</margin> they use only <term>machanae</term> <gloss>broad, oblong wooden swords</gloss> and javelins and fire-hardened spears against their enemies.

From the living Pacra, where his family members collected gold could never be extorted by any enticements, threats, or tortures. When asked where he had that—for thirty pounds of gold had been taken from his treasury—he answered that his family members who used to collect gold from those mountains in the time of his parents and his own were dead. <margin>30 pounds of gold from Pacra.</margin> He had had no concern since he passed puberty for searching for gold. He could never be pulled from this proposed institution. From this severity toward Pacra, Vasco reconciled the minds of the neighboring chieftains to himself. Hence it arose that...

<summary>This page describes the capture of a tiger and the brutal execution of the chieftain Pacra, who was fed to war dogs by Vasco Núñez de Balboa. It also details the effectiveness of Spanish dogs in battle and the natives' lack of interest in gold mining.</summary>
